name: Fractora RF

lead: Fractora is a fractional radiofrequency handpiece from InMode, used in clinics for skin tightening, acne scars and oil production. Morpheus8 was later modified from this platform.

Arrays of pins deliver bipolar RF energy into the skin in a fractional pattern, heating tissue to prompt collagen remodeling. Studies are small prospective and retrospective ones, some combining Fractora with other RF treatments such as FaceTite, plus a sebum trial.

paras: It is a clinic treatment, done in a series of sessions and sometimes combined with other RF devices. Results are described as gradual as skin remodels.
Redness, swelling and pinpoint bleeding are commonly reported for RF microneedling. Fractora-specific adverse data were limited in the sources, and it is a clinic-only procedure.

angle.text: Fractora sends fractional RF through pins into the skin, prompting collagen remodeling and less oil for tighter skin and softer acne scars. It preceded Morpheus8 and has been studied in small, mostly early studies.

lead: Fractora is a fractional bipolar radiofrequency (RF) handpiece from InMode that delivers RF energy through arrays of pins placed on the skin, a microneedling-type approach. It was the platform that InMode later modified and marketed as Morpheus8 [1][2]. People have it done to tighten loose skin on the lower face and neck, to smooth atrophic acne scars and to reduce oil production, with the aim of a firmer, smoother and clearer-looking face [2][3][4].

Treatment is a clinic procedure. The pins create small zones of RF-heated tissue in the skin, and the body responds by remodelling collagen over the following weeks. The 2019 Aesthetic Surgery Journal supplement describes RF microneedling with adjustable depth as allowing subdermal adipose remodelling as well as skin tightening, and positions it for patients in a treatment gap: not severe enough for excisional surgery, but beyond what noninvasive devices alone achieve [2].
Published work is mostly small prospective and retrospective studies, many combining Fractora with other InMode RF devices such as FaceTite and BodyTite.
infobox: Facial and neck laxity, atrophic acne scars, sebum production [1][3]

paras: Fractora is a fractional bipolar RF system. Instead of treating the whole surface, a tip carrying a grid of pins delivers RF energy at discrete points, leaving untreated skin between them to speed recovery. Tips studied include a 24-pin coated version [3]. Adjustable depth lets the clinician place the energy in the dermis and deeper tissue [2].

Fractora modified to Morpheus8 is the name used in the plastic surgery literature for the later-generation handpiece, so studies of Morpheus8 describe closely related technology [1][2]. Grokipedia, an AI-generated reference, lists redness, swelling and pinpoint bleeding as the general reactions after Morpheus8 treatment.

The 2019 supplement describes combining adjustable-depth fractional RF with bipolar RF to treat laxity in three groups: younger patients who want soft-tissue tightening without scars or downtime, patients with laxity too severe for liposuction-with-contraction alone but not enough for excision, and those with recurrent laxity after prior surgery [2]. A 2014 Clinics in Plastic Surgery review of nonexcisional, minimally invasive neck rejuvenation covers this class of devices [5].

A single-center prospective, evaluator-blinded trial in 2022 tested three monthly sessions with a Fractora 24-pin coated tip. Sebumeter readings showed a significant fall in sebum production from the first treatment, sustained through the study, and biopsies showed lower density and size of sebaceous glands. Acne scar volume fell significantly, without a significant rise in melanin levels, which authors noted as relevant to pigmentation risk [3].

A retrospective multicentre study (2013 to 2018) in Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery Global Open evaluated a combination of bipolar RF (FaceTite) and fractional bipolar RF (Fractora modified to Morpheus8) for lower face and neck laxity in 247 patients (234 women, 13 men; average age 55.1 years, average BMI 24.3, 9 percent smokers). It collected Baker Face/Neck classification, energy used, adverse events and satisfaction, and included four cadaver dissections to relate the underlying anatomy to the RF treatment [1].
The 2019 Aesthetic Surgery Journal supplement is a description of the technique and its rationale for the combined treatment rather than a controlled trial [2].

The 2022 prospective trial examined sebum and acne scars after three sessions [3]. A registered comparison in darker skin (NCT03380845, four participants, completed, started 2018) compared a 1,550-nm laser with fractional RF microneedling for acne scars [4].

Adverse-event details specific to Fractora are reported in the multimodal retrospective review [1]. General RF microneedling reactions described for Morpheus8 include redness, swelling and pinpoint bleeding. The acne-scar trial reported no significant increase in melanin after treatment [3].

Fractora and Morpheus8 belong to the group of RF and microneedling procedures that people in appearance communities discuss as alternatives to surgical facelifts and neck lifts. InMode, the manufacturer, is also the company behind FaceTite and BodyTite, which are the devices paired with Fractora in the published combination studies [1][2].

timeline.event: Start of the period covered by the multicentre retrospective study of combined bipolar and fractional RF [1].
Review of nonexcisional neck rejuvenation published in Clinics in Plastic Surgery [5].
A registered comparison of laser and fractional RF microneedling for acne scars in darker skin begins [4].
Aesthetic Surgery Journal supplement describes combined adjustable-depth fractional RF and bipolar RF [2].
Multimodal RF retrospective review of 247 patients is published [1].
Prospective trial reports lower sebum production and reduced acne scar volume after Fractora 24-pin sessions [3].
